Stability of preferences across ranking stages

Source: R/rologit.R
rank_test.Rd

Tests the assumption of the rank-ordered logit that the relative preference for two alternatives is the same at every stage of the ranking: the model is refit with a second set of coefficients for the stages after position after (every coefficient, including the constants), and the hypothesis that the two sets are equal is tested by the likelihood ratio, as Hausman and Ruud (1987, section 3) do, and by the Wald statistic, as Allison and Christakis (1994, section 5.4) do; both are chi-square with as many degrees of freedom as the model has parameters. A coefficient that one block of stages does not identify (an alternative that no ranking orders there, such as one always ranked within the first after positions) is left out of both statistics and their degrees of freedom, with a warning; a penalized fit (firth = TRUE or a prior) is then refused, since its fit with separate early and late coefficients has no finite penalty. Chapman and Staelin's (1982) pooling test is the sequential version that compares the first \(E\) stages with stage \(E + 1\). Within a tie group the stages take the positions of each order in the sum over orders.

Usage

rank_test(object, after = 1L)

Arguments

object

A rologit() fit.

after

The last position of the early stages (default 1: the first choice against the rest of the ranking).

Value

A data frame of class "iia_test" with the LR and Wald rows (statistic, df, p.value); the attribute "coefficients" holds the early and late estimates and their difference with its standard error. The Wald statistic uses the fit's covariance type (analytic for a bootstrap fit).

Details

A rejection says that later rankings follow different coefficients. That can mean careless ranking further down (the coefficients then shrink towards zero in the late stages, the reading of Chapman and Staelin and of Hausman and Ruud) or a change in valuation; Allison and Christakis also note that apparent differences between stages can arise from heterogeneity across respondents rather than from a change within respondents. Fitting with depth = after uses only the early stages.

The likelihood-ratio statistic assumes independent rankings (a fit's cluster does not enter it); the Wald statistic uses the fit's covariance, cluster-robust when the fit has one. Their chi-square reference is asymptotic; with few rankings per coefficient it can be far off, and no parametric bootstrap of this test is offered. The split design (separate coefficients after the first stage) is outside separation()'s scope: when a split fit's data are separated, its maximum-likelihood statistic uses the value where its optimizer stopped, not the supremum (the penalized form is unaffected).

References

Allison, P.D. and Christakis, N.A. (1994). Logit models for sets of ranked items. Sociological Methodology, 24, 199-228. doi:10.2307/270983

Chapman, R.G. and Staelin, R. (1982). Exploiting rank ordered choice set data within the stochastic utility model. Journal of Marketing Research, 19, 288-301. doi:10.1177/002224378201900302

Hausman, J.A. and Ruud, P.A. (1987). Specifying and testing econometric models for rank-ordered data. Journal of Econometrics, 34, 83-104. doi:10.1016/0304-4076(87)90068-6

See also

rologit()

Other specification tests: captivity_test(), combine_test(), hl_test(), term_test()

Examples

set.seed(5)
d <- rrologit(800, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1), c = c(-0.3, 0.6), d = c(0.2, 0.4)))
rank_test(rologit(rank ~ 1 | x1, data = d, id = "id", alt = "alt"))
#> Stability of preferences across ranking stages (position 1 against later; 800 ranking(s) with later stages) 
#>              test statistic df p.value
#>  Likelihood ratio     7.771  6   0.255
#>              Wald     7.756  6   0.257
